The summer I was twelve, my aunt Ilse rebuilt the old wood kiln behind her house in Hesk. Her teacher, Mr. Varga, had fired it for forty years and left her his notes when he died that winter. She relaid the firebox from his own drawings. The first load would hold a tall jar Mr. Osgood had ordered for the mill's hundredth year, in a blue he had picked from a test tile.

We lit it at dawn. Ilse fed the firebox and watched the fire through the spyhole; my job was to carry wood in from the shed, armload after armload. Once she let me look through the spyhole. At dusk Mr. Osgood helped her cover the woodpile with a tarp. She had promised I could stay up all night, and she kept her promise.

Near midnight the storm came, hissing on the chimney cap, and the fire began to sink. Ilse read the notes to herself and found a night thirty years back when Varga had brought a firing through worse rain by closing the damper halfway and feeding slowly. She had meant to set his notes aside and do the first firing her own way. Now she followed them exactly. When I begged to feed the fire by feel, she said the book would teach me first. I was the one who fretted that Mr. Osgood would take only the blue of his tile.

Two days later we took down the bricked-up door with Mr. Osgood watching. The jar came out furred with grey ash. Before anyone could wipe it, Ilse tapped it with her knuckle, listening for any flaw the eye might miss, a crack under the glaze, and it rang clear, the note she had hoped for. Then she brushed off the ash, and there was the exact color of his tile. Mr. Osgood carried it down to the mill himself.

The jar still stands in the mill window. When strangers stop to admire it, I tell them I carried every stick of wood that fired it, whether or not they have asked, and I tell it well.

The summer I was twelve, my aunt Ilse rebuilt the old wood kiln behind her house in Hesk. Her teacher, Mr. Varga, had fired it for forty years and left her his notes when he died that winter. She relaid the firebox wider than his, to take longer logs. The first load would hold a tall jar Mr. Osgood had ordered for the mill's hundredth year, in a blue he had picked from a test tile.

We lit it at dawn. Ilse carried the wood and fed the firebox herself; my job was to watch the fire through the spyhole and call out its color. Once I fetched an armload from the shed. At dusk Mr. Osgood helped her cover the woodpile with a tarp. Whatever doubts she had, Ilse kept them from me.

Near midnight the storm came, hissing on the chimney cap, and the fire began to sink. Ilse read aloud from the notes: in worse rain, Varga had closed the damper halfway, fed slowly, and brought his firing through. Then she set the book aside. 'His firebox was a narrow little thing,' she said, and threw on two more logs. She had meant to follow him exactly for this first firing. When I asked to feed it, she said the book would teach me first. My own worry was that Mr. Osgood would take only the blue of his tile.

Two days later we took down the bricked-up door with Mr. Osgood watching. Under the ash the color was right, the exact blue of his tile, but a crack, a flaw any eye could see, ran from rim to foot. Ilse tapped it with her knuckle, hoping the crack went only through the glaze, and it gave back a dull thud. Mr. Osgood offered to buy it as it was, and she turned him down.

The jar stood on Ilse's workshop shelf until she died; now it stands on mine, crack to the wall. That night I had watched it glow whiter than the rest and called out only the color of the fire. I still go back over that hour more often than I would like.

We lit it at dawn. Ilse carried in the wood from the shed and watched the fire through the spyhole, and she gave me the firebox to feed, which was my job until dawn came round again. Once, while she ate, I watched the spyhole for her. At dusk Mr. Osgood helped her cover the woodpile with a tarp, and a long story about the mill kept him at our gate till dark.

Near midnight the storm came, hissing on the chimney cap, and the fire began to sink. Ilse read the notes to herself, found where Varga had brought a firing through worse rain by closing the damper halfway and feeding slowly, and set the book aside. 'You'll learn this by feel or not at all,' she said, and left the poker in my hands. I had expected her to follow him exactly for a first firing. I fed it fast and wild, and forgot my fear that Mr. Osgood would take only the blue of his tile.

Two days later we took down the bricked-up door with Mr. Osgood watching. Ash I had stirred up had blown across the jar and melted into the glaze, turning the blue of his tile the color of a frog's back, a strange speckled green. Ilse tapped it with her knuckle, listening for any flaw the eye might miss, a crack under the glaze, and it rang clear. Mr. Osgood laughed until he had to sit down, then paid her double.

He named it the Pickle, and the Pickle has stood in the mill window ever since. Children count its spots through the glass. Whenever I walk past, I catch myself grinning back at it like a fool.

The summer I was twelve, my aunt Ilse rebuilt the old wood kiln behind her house in Hesk. Her teacher, Mr. Varga, had fired it for forty years and left her his notes when he died that winter. She relaid the firebox from his own drawings. The first load would hold a tall jar Mr. Osgood had ordered for the mill's hundredth year, in a blue he had picked from a test tile.

We lit it at dawn. Ilse carried the wood from the shed and fed the firebox, watching the fire through the spyhole, and my job was to read Varga's notes aloud to her, line by line. Once, near dawn, she let me feed in a log. At dusk Mr. Osgood helped her cover the woodpile with a tarp, while the hens she kept behind the shed fussed at the smoke.

Near midnight a soft rain came, barely enough to darken the bricks, and the fire never faltered. It was the easiest firing Ilse could remember, yet she followed his notes exactly as I read them out. 'The first one belongs to him,' she said. The notes told how he had once brought a firing through a far worse storm, and her firebox was laid to his plan. Learning by feel, she told me, would come after I had learned the book. As for the blue, Mr. Osgood had said any shade near his tile would please him.

Two days later we took down the bricked-up door with Mr. Osgood watching. Under the ash the jar was the exact color of his tile, without a mark on it. Ilse tapped it with her knuckle, and instead of a ring it gave back a dull note: somewhere under the glaze was a hairline crack, a flaw the eye could not find. She looked at me once. Then she wrapped the jar in sacking and took Mr. Osgood's money.

Mr. Osgood died believing it perfect, and the jar still stands in the front hall of the mill. Whenever I pass the open door, I look in at it, half expecting to find it lying in pieces on the floor.

She relaid the firebox from his own drawings. The first load would hold a tall jar Mr. Osgood had ordered for the mill's hundredth year, in a blue he had picked from a test tile.

We lit it at dawn. Ilse carried in the wood from the shed, fed the firebox and watched the fire through the spyhole, reading Varga's notes to herself. Once she had me read a line aloud when her eyes were smarting. My job was to cover the woodpile with the tarp and tug it straight whenever the wind lifted a corner. She kept the driest logs for the last hours.

Near midnight a soft rain came, barely enough to darken the bricks, and the fire never faltered. Ilse had meant to set his notes aside and do the first firing her own way, but she followed them to the letter. 'Mr. Osgood chose that blue from a tile,' she said, 'and that blue is what he will get.' The notes told how Varga had once brought a firing through a far worse storm, and her firebox was laid to his plan. Learning by feel, she told me, would come after I had learned the book.

Two days later we took down the bricked-up door with Mr. Osgood watching. Under the ash the jar was the exact color of his tile. He looked at it a long while, then turned it down: the mill's new owners wanted a clock in the window, and he had no use for a jar. Ilse tapped it with her knuckle, listening for any flaw the eye might miss, a crack under the glaze, and it rang clear. He paid for the clay and left it with us.

The jar holds umbrellas in my hallway now. Guests sometimes admire it, and I have to look twice to remember which jar they mean. Most days I walk past it with my coat half on.

Every January for thirty-one years, Tomas Brill, a retired signalman, has carried a torch and a pencil notebook into the disused Pellow railway tunnel to count the bats asleep on its walls. In that time the colony has grown, with only the occasional fall, from forty to nearly three hundred, with a smaller winter roost at the old lime kilns in Fennick, half a mile down the valley. For years visitors forced their way in and lit fires inside the tunnel, so two autumns ago the county council fitted a steel gate to protect the bats: upright bars, with gaps wide enough for a bat but too narrow for a person, above a solid steel panel. That January Brill counted 168 bats.

Ruth Okafor, the county ecologist, spent her first week phoning farmers about the dry summer, asking how the moths and midges had fared, since bats that find little to eat go into winter thin. She also hung temperature loggers along the tunnel and two more in the kilns.

The farmers' answers were ordinary; the loggers were the surprise. All winter the kilns stayed cold, while the air behind the gate ran three degrees warmer. Brill's notebooks, which record the air temperature at the tunnel mouth every January, showed a reading higher than any in thirty-one years. The solid panel was blocking the cold air that once moved in along the floor. With the fires gone the bats were undisturbed, yet the warmth kept rousing them, and each waking burned fat they needed to survive until spring. Okafor found the missing bats dead beneath their ledges.

The council answered within a fortnight. In March workmen settled a new gate onto the old hinges, with the same bars and the panel cut away, and by the next winter Okafor's loggers matched Brill's old January figures. His latest count was 236. Councils are seldom quick to admit that a scheme meant to protect wildlife did the opposite; this one said so in its first statement, covered the cost from its own budget, and asked Brill to keep counting.

Every January for thirty-one years, Tomas Brill, a retired signalman, has carried a torch and a pencil notebook into the disused Pellow railway tunnel to count the bats asleep on its walls. In that time the colony has grown, with only the occasional fall, from forty to nearly three hundred, with a smaller winter roost at the old lime kilns in Fennick, half a mile down the valley. For years visitors forced their way in and lit fires inside the tunnel, so two autumns ago the county council fitted a steel gate to protect the bats: upright bars, with gaps wide enough for a bat but too narrow for a person, above a solid steel panel. That January Brill counted 168 bats.

Ruth Okafor, the county ecologist, had a suspect before she reached the valley. The gate had at least ended the fires, but she hung her temperature loggers behind its solid panel, where any trapped warmth would gather first, and asked Brill to count the kilns as well, to see whether the bats had moved there.

The loggers read a steady four degrees all winter, as cold as the tunnel had ever been, and the kilns, which visitors leave undisturbed, had suffered the same fall, losing two bats in every five. The pattern was in Brill's notebooks. In 1995, 2006 and 2018 a dry summer had been followed by a thin January count, and each time the colony recovered within three winters. Bats that find few insects in a dry summer enter hibernation without enough fat to survive it, and the missing bats had never woken.

That explanation settled the councillors, who agreed that the gate could stay and the file could close. Brill has kept reading his own pages. The dry summers in them come closer together with each decade, and a colony that loses two bats in five can rebuild over three winters only if the summers between are wet. What the colony does after two dry summers in a row is a question his notebooks have yet to answer. Brill will be eighty in the spring, and he has begun teaching a neighbour's daughter to count.

Every January for thirty-one years, Tomas Brill, a retired signalman, has carried a torch and a pencil notebook into the disused Pellow railway tunnel to count the bats asleep on its walls. In that time the colony has grown, with only the occasional fall, from forty to nearly three hundred, with a smaller winter roost at the old lime kilns in Fennick, half a mile down the valley. For years visitors forced their way in and lit fires inside the tunnel, so two autumns ago the county council fitted a steel gate to protect the bats: upright bars, with gaps wide enough for a bat but too narrow for a person, above a solid steel panel. That January Brill counted 168 bats.

Ruth Okafor, the county ecologist, knew the gate had ended the fires, and she wondered what else it kept out. She spent her first evenings beside it with a bat detector, counting how many bats passed between the bars and how many turned away. She also weighed a few sleepers and hung temperature loggers along the tunnel.

The bats slipped through the gaps without slowing. The ones she weighed were far from thin despite the dry summer, fat enough to survive, and the loggers showed the warmest stretch of the tunnel as cold as ever. The answer was in the margins of Brill's notebooks, where he had always jotted his counts from the Fennick kilns, a roost visitors leave undisturbed. Twice before, the tunnel count had dropped by about a hundred while the kilns rose by the same amount, and both times the colony moved back within two winters. This January the kilns held 132 bats, against their usual thirty. The colony as a whole had suffered no fall; the missing bats had gone down the valley.

By then the council's working group had met four times, ordered drawings for a new gate with wider gaps, and issued a statement promising to protect the colony "whatever the cost." The bats had settled the kilns weeks before the first meeting, and Brill expects them home in a winter or two, by which time the drawings may be ready.

Every January for thirty-one years, Tomas Brill, a retired signalman, has carried a torch and a pencil notebook into the disused Pellow railway tunnel to count the bats asleep on its walls. In that time the colony has grown, with only the occasional fall, from forty to nearly three hundred, with a smaller winter roost at the old lime kilns in Fennick, half a mile down the valley. For years visitors forced their way in and lit fires inside the tunnel, so two autumns ago the county council fitted a steel gate to protect the bats: upright bars, with gaps wide enough for a bat but too narrow for a person, above a solid steel panel. That January Brill counted 391 bats.

Ruth Okafor, the county ecologist, drove first to the Fennick kilns and spent three evenings there counting the bats as they left at dusk. She also hung temperature loggers along the tunnel.

The kilns held their usual sixty; not one was missing. That sent her to Brill's notebooks. Beside each count he had written down every fire he found in the tunnel, and the colony had grown fastest in the rare winters free of fires. The kilns, ungated, still see fires most winters, and their colony has stayed at sixty for a decade. Her loggers showed the tunnel steady and cold, without the warm spikes a fire leaves. Even after a dry summer that left them thin, the bats in the tunnel, undisturbed by smoke for the first time in years, had simply survived the winter.

By then the gate was gone. Walkers who had used the tunnel as a shortcut complained about the long way round, and the council moved quickly: in April, two months before Okafor's figures were ready, it settled the contractor's account for taking it down. In November Brill found fresh ashes on the tunnel floor, and this January he counted 302. Okafor's report sits in the council's files, and the empty hinges are still fixed in the wall. One more season of patience would have kept the gate.

Every January for thirty-one years, Tomas Brill, a retired signalman, has carried a torch and a pencil notebook into the disused Pellow railway tunnel to count the bats asleep on its walls. In that time the colony has grown, with only the occasional fall, from forty to nearly three hundred, with a smaller winter roost at the old lime kilns in Fennick, half a mile down the valley. For years visitors forced their way in and lit fires inside the tunnel, so two autumns ago the county council fitted a steel gate to protect the bats: upright bars, with gaps wide enough for a bat but too narrow for a person, above a solid steel panel. That January Brill counted 168 bats.

Ruth Okafor, the county ecologist, began on her knees on the tunnel floor, sifting the old hearths with a trowel and holding each pinch of ash up to her torch to judge how fresh it was. She also hung temperature loggers along the tunnel.

Brill's notebooks explained what she found. Since the gate went up he had noted, visit by visit, places where visitors had forced the bars apart, each gap wide enough for a person to squeeze through. The loggers caught sudden bursts of warmth in the cold air on weekend nights, and each fire woke bats that needed every scrap of fat to survive until spring; the missing bats lay dead beneath their ledges. They had been far from thin, since the dry summer had been a good one for moths. None had moved to the Fennick kilns, which visitors leave undisturbed and where the count had held at sixty.

Okafor's report settled the matter in March: weld the bars and fit a stronger frame. The council accepted it, then waited eighteen months for a welder. In that time Brill reported three more forced gaps and two more fires, each by letter, and each letter brought back the same printed card thanking him for his interest in council services. The welder came in September. Brill counted 121 bats in January.
